title: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed in West Bank shooting
description: At least four Palestinians and two Israelis have been killed in a shooting in the occupied West Bank - the deadliest single incident there in months.T
body: At least four Palestinians and two Israelis have been killed in a shooting in the occupied West Bank - the deadliest single incident there in months.There are conflicting accounts of the sequence of events in the northern village of Tal. Palestinians told the BBC that residents confronted Jewish settlers who were attacking them. An eyewitness said soldiers then arrived and started shooting. Israel's military said it had responded to reports that hikers had been attacked. It said "terrorists stole the weapon" of a security guard and killed him. It later said a soldier had also been killed, but did not give details. The IDF has not explained who killed the other Palestinians.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) says it is preparing for a major operation in the area and has cancelled soldiers' leave. There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.Ahmed Zeidan, an eyewitness, told the BBC the latest incident began early in the morning, when locals in Tal rushed to confront about 30 settlers who were attacking Palestinian homes. He said hand-to-hand clashes broke out in the presence of Israeli soldiers. A local leader of the ruling Palestinian Authority's Fatah party, Essam Saifi, told Reuters news agency that settlers opened fire before Israeli forces arrived and also started shooting.He said two brothers and two of their cousins were among those killed. Palestinian officials said several other Palestinians were wounded.The IDF said Palestinians began the attack.It said soldiers had gone to Tal following a report of an attack on Israeli civilians who were hiking in the area - part of which falls in an area of the West Bank under full control of the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the other part under PA administrative control and Israeli security control.The military says that the hike was not co-ordinated with them.  A security guard from a nearby settler outpost had gone to the scene and had his gun snatched by a Palestinian who used it against the Israelis, killing him, the IDF says. Soldiers then "eliminated the terrorist who executed the terror attack", the IDF added. Two video clips have been widely shared by local media - but not independently verified.  One appears to show a confrontation between Palestinians and Israeli soldiers and armed Israelis dressed in civilian clothes as gunshots are fired and a group of Israeli civilians, including children, watch and heckle. Armed Israelis in civilian clothes then push and kick back two Palestinian men.  The second video shot from a different angle appears to show that both men tried to grab the guns - one of them successfully.  There is a chaotic scene and several gunshots can be heard as he appears to fire it and troops also respond.The IDF has said a 27-year-old soldier "fell during operational activity in the area of ​​the village". The circumstances of his death remain unclear. The Israeli ambulance service said two Israelis were also wounded.The Palestinian foreign ministry said it "condemns in the strongest terms the massacre" in Tal.It said "the escalation of settler terrorism is a direct consequence of the protection, political backing, and complete impunity granted by the Israeli government and occupation forces". "Official Israeli incitement continues to fuel and encourage these crimes, creating an environment in which settler violence flourishes without accountability," it added.An AFP reporter at the site, south-west of Nablus, said roadblocks had been set up and troops were searching for additional suspects. The IDF later said it raided a hospital in Nablus and "apprehended two terrorists who took part in the shooting attack" and who had gone to the hospital for treatment.Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to act "with full force against the terrorists and those who orchestrate and sponsor them".He called an emergency meeting with security officials, and reinforcements have been sent to the area, close to the settlement of Havat Gilad.Netanyahu's office issued a joint statement with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying the home of the Palestinian shooter in Tal would be demolished and that the legalisation of unauthorised settler outposts and the establishment of new ones would be speeded up.Outposts are wildcat settlements, often just a cluster of caravans set up on a hilltop. They are illegal under international law and also Israeli law when they are built without official approval.On X, Yair Golan, the leader of Israel's Democrats Party - who is a reserve major general in the IDF - described the joint statement from Netanyahu and Katz as "a clear intent to set the area ablaze".After the attack in Tal, there have been reports of violent confrontations between dozens of armed settlers and Palestinians in other nearby villages in the northern West Bank. A number of Palestinians have been wounded with one shot in the head in Farata, local medics say.Since October 2023, 1,114 Palestinians have been killed there, the vast majority by the IDF, the UN says. It says at least 35 of the deaths have involved attacks by settlers.The UN says 41 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war.Israel has built hundreds settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law.

schema.headline: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed in West Bank shooting

title: LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers after Los Angeles Lakers exit
description: LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.The 41-year-ol
body: LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.The 41-year-old, the highest points scorer in the history of the league, left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight years last month.  The Cleveland Cavaliers, Golden State Warriors, Minnesota Timberwolves and Miami Heat were also rumored to be in the running for the four-time NBA champion."I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fanbase and start this incredible journey one last time," James said on X., externalJames has won an NBA title with all three teams he previously played for. He won two with Miami, who earlier this week mistakenly posted a link to an 'introductory press conference' for James.A Heat spokesperson told Reuters, external the video was posted in error by staff who were preparing for the possibility of James rejoining the team he played for between 2010 and 2014.Either side of that, James had two spells with Cleveland, who drafted James in 2003 and are based near his hometown of Akron, Ohio."Miami I'll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always [be] home," James added.James helped the Cavs become NBA champions in 2016 and joined the Lakers in 2018, claiming another NBA title two years later.He has been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player four times, all between 2009 and 2013, and is a 22-time NBA All-Star.

schema.headline: LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers after Los Angeles Lakers exit

title: EA FC 27: FUT leads to new age rating after loot box rule change
description: EA FC gets a new age rating after loot box rule changesImage source, EAImage caption, Kylian Mbappé is the cover star of the upcoming EA FC 27ByTom Ri
body: EA FC gets a new age rating after loot box rule changesImage source, EAImage caption, Kylian Mbappé is the cover star of the upcoming EA FC 27ByTom RichardsonBBC Newsbeat EA FC is one of the most popular video game series in the world, and reliably tops the UK charts each year.And as the trailer for the latest instalment of the annual football simulator dropped this week, one new addition drew a lot of attention.A 16+ age rating.Previously, the game had been marked as 3+, meaning its content was considered suitable for most players.But last month the scope of those age ratings expanded to cover elements of the online experience including in-game purchases and mechanisms designed to encourage repeat play.In the case of EA FC, one of its most popular features has come under the new rules.Image source, EAImage caption, Ultimate Team is based around collectible cards featuring player statisticsUltimate Team, commonly referred to as FUT, is one of the main modes of the EA FC series.Players can spend money on virtual card packs containing a random selection of star footballers to build a dream squad.It is possible to trade the cards and build up in-game "coins" without using real money, but it is generally seen as a slower and less effective way to play.Earlier this year The Pan-European Game Information body (PEGI), announced it was overhauling its age-rating system used in 38 countries including the UK. It made the decision to brand any game containing so-called loot boxes - "paid random items" - as a PEGI 16 by default. EA FC falls under the new rules due to the inclusion of FUT, earning it the higher rating. Critics have compared FUT and similar modes in other games to gambling, with recent research finding they "blurred the lines".Electronic Arts, the game's publisher, has pushed back on the claims and stressed players don't need to spend money to participate in FUT.The UK government chose not to bring loot boxes under the Gambling Act 2005, external, saying there was no evidence of a "causative link" to harms.Despite the criticisms, FUT and other loot box-style modes remain popular.According to EA's latest financial report, , externalFUT was responsible for a "substantial portion" of the $5.5bn annual revenue it made from selling add-on content for its games.What does it mean for players?Image source, EAImage caption, EA FC 26 was the best-selling video game in the UK last yearA PEGI rating prevents underage customers from walking into a shop and buying a product considered unsuitable for them.In reality, the vast majority of video game purchases are now made digitally, although most major online stores provide safeguards.In-game, most platforms and titles offer parental controls, and EA FC automatically restricts purchases on accounts belonging to players under 13.Before the new rules were brought in, the decision on a game's rating was based on its content, rather than its online features.Ultimately, the decision on whether under-16s can play the new edition will rest with parents.UKIE, the trade body for the British Games Industry, said "PEGI ratings exist to give parents, players and retailers clear, independent guidance on the content of a game"."The rating system is kept under regular review to reflect how games and their features evolve, and this update means parents can be confident the same protections apply here as with any other game carrying that rating," a spokesperson said.Other new additionsThe new headline feature of EA FC 27 is "The Grounds" - an open-world area where players can hone their skills and get tips from "mentors" including cover star Kylian Mbappé and Lioness Chloe Kelly.Alex Hunter, the character first introduced to the series in FIFA 17, returns this year as one of the experienced players dishing out advice.EA has also promised gameplay tweaks to attacking movement and the behaviour of computer-controlled opponents.As in previous years, it plans to reveal more details about those changes in the run-up to the game's release, which is expected to land around September.The introduction of a new Ultimate Plus Edition - which grants players a host of perks and access to the game one week before its official release - also raised eyebrows because of its £139.99 price tag.EA is currently in the process of being bought for $55bn by a group of investors led by Saudi Arabia.BBC Newsbeat has approached the company for a comment on the PEGI rating and criticisms of the Ultimate Plus Edition price.Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: EA FC 27: FUT leads to new age rating after loot box rule change

title: Jurgen Klopp: Germany boss threatens to quit new job if media invade family's privacy
description: Jurgen Klopp started his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.The former Liverpool manager w
body: Jurgen Klopp started his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.The former Liverpool manager was appointed on a four-year deal on Friday to replace Julian Nagelsmann, who resigned this month after Germany's shock World Cup defeat by Paraguay in the last 32.But the 59-year-old issued a warning to the media as he held his first news conference as Germany's head coach."If you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace then I'll be gone, I'll just turn away," Klopp said."I know there are other countries where national team coaches are treated even worse."I'm not doing this job for myself, I'm doing it for you. I'm taking this job even though I've seen how you've treated Julian Nagelsmann and Thomas Tuchel."I love this job but I am always ready to call it quits if need be."Both Nagelsmann and England boss Tuchel came under media scrutiny after their exits from the World Cup, with Tuchel criticised for his defensive tactics and substitutions as the Three Lions let slip a 1-0 lead in their semi-final defeat by Argentina.Klopp's appointment was widely expected for weeks and his contract will see him through to the 2030 World Cup, co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco."Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any 'career' after the national team," he added. "This is the pinnacle, the absolutely high point of my footballing career as coach. I will give everything I have got."

schema.headline: Jurgen Klopp: Germany boss threatens to quit new job if media invade family's privacy

title: Uganda's Ghetto Kids: Dancing with Shakira and Burna Boy at the World Cup 'very, very, very, very, very good'
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The children say dancing on stage with Shakira and Burna Boy was a dream come trueByNatasha Booty and BBC Wor
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The children say dancing on stage with Shakira and Burna Boy was a dream come trueByNatasha Booty and BBC World ServiceUgandan dance group the Ghetto Kids are celebrating another milestone after appearing at the football World Cup final half-time show on Sunday - a life-changing experience summed up by 10-year-old Sierra as "very, very, very, very, very good".Despite critics bemoaning the addition of a Superbowl-style performance , externalto the beautiful game's biggest event, the children's performance alongside global stars Burna Boy and Shakira was viewed by many millions around the world.Speaking to the BBC's Newsday programme, the young members of the dance troupe and their manager say that rising from humble beginnings in Uganda's capital, Kampala, then finding fame while balancing it all with schoolwork has taken perseverance."Never give up... pray to God. Listen to your parents, education is first, that's all," says Sierra. She and 11-year-old Josephine are still on a high, after their World Cup appearance midway through the game that saw Spain beat Argentina at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey."I saw Messi and Lamine Yamal!" says Josephine about the two team's stars - Argentinian captain Lionel Messi and Spain's teenage winger Yamal."I was so happy to see Messi and people watching us. I felt so excited and I was smiling, and a little bit nervous," she recalls."Shakira, she's very kind," chimes in Sierra.Figure caption, Stars shine at half-time showThe children gave Colombian pop star Shakira and Nigerian musician Burna Boy a big hug on stage as their performance ended - a moment their manager, Dauda Kavuma, insists was a natural show of affection, rather than clever choreography.Learning they had been picked to perform was a dream come true. The children "ran around in a circle, banging and shouting" when they learned the news, says Kavuma."They had already danced to Waka Waka, external in Britain's Got Talent," he explains about Shakira's remake of the 1980s Cameroonian classic Zangaléwa by Golden Sounds, external."But it was now a great moment to see that Shakira invited us... to perform with her."It means a lot and it's life-changing."Kavuma's philosophy is that there is so much talent in the ghetto, you just have to polish it.As a child he lived on the streets of Uganda's capital before the kindness of a teacher changed his life.He wanted to give back and later became a teacher himself before creating the Ghetto Kids dance troupe - formed of homeless children and those who could not afford school fees. Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Frequent practice is a part of life for the Ghetto Kids, who have a huge social media followingCombining a multitude of African dance styles, comedy and pure joy, they soon caught the attention of Ugandan musicians including Eddy Kenzo, who asked them to feature in some of his videos.The group's strategy has involved harnessing the viral-making powers of the internet, and their biggest break followed in 2017 when they appeared in the music video for French Montana's song Unforgettable - which at the time of writing has amassed more than 1.9 billion views on YouTube, external. That recognition opened yet more doors, leading the Ghetto Kids to the final of Britain's Got Talent in 2023, before also competing in America's Got Talent the following year. It has also enabled Kavuma to expand his project offering housing, food and tuition to many children across Uganda.This year's football World Cup final may have been the Ghetto Kids' biggest stage yet, but it was not their first major sporting event.Back in 2023, the Ghetto Kids were thrilled to meet Kylian Mbappé and perform at a football half-time match in France between rivals Paris Saint-Germain and Reims.Another recent career highlight was a film being made about their story, called Ghetto Kids Documentary: No Plan B.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, "Education first" is the message their parents and manager have drilled into the young dancersDespite their fame, the children's parents and manager have instilled in them an "education-first" mentality.Videos for their vast social media following are filmed at weekends, so that weekdays are largely kept free for school, Kavuma says. If they have to travel for performances, the children connect online to their teachers while away and catch up on any missed work once back in Kampala.Both Sierra and Josephine tell the BBC they plan to become doctors when they grow up but will never give up their passion for dance."Dancing changed my life - I went to school because of dance," says Sierra.Josephine agrees: "Dance is what I know and that makes me happy because that's my talent."So, what do they want to say to other children who, like them, might be talented but have not had the easiest start in life?"To love themselves, believe in God, and pray. Be with their talents - don't deny them," answers Josephine."And we love them."Image source, Getty Images for Global CitizenImage caption, Big hugs from Burna Boy and Shakira at the halftime showYou may also be interested in:

schema.headline: Uganda's Ghetto Kids: Dancing with Shakira and Burna Boy at the World Cup 'very, very, very, very, very good'

title: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton leads Charles Leclerc in Ferrari one-two in Friday practice
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lewis Hamilton has won the Hungarian Grand Prix a record eight timesByF1 Correspondent at the HungaroringUpdated 3
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lewis Hamilton has won the Hungarian Grand Prix a record eight timesByF1 Correspondent at the HungaroringUpdated 36 minutes agoLewis Hamilton led team-mate Charles Leclerc to a Ferrari one-two in Friday practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix.Hamilton was 0.148 seconds ahead of Leclerc, with McLaren's Lando Norris third, 0.499secs off the pace, and Red Bull's Max Verstappen fourth.Fernando Alonso ended the day 19th fastest in the new Aston Martin after what team principal Adrian Newey said was a "promising" first outing for a car that is new apart from its engine, gearbox and front suspension.Alonso was 2.990secs off the pace, but had a lap nearly 0.4secs faster ruled out for track limits at the final corner.Although that is still a long way from competitiveness, it is a significant step forward from where Aston Martin have spent most of the season.Ferrari looked in good shape, as might have been expected on a track that lends itself to the car's strong cornering performance.But Mercedes, with George Russell in fifth 0.933secs off the pace and championship leader Kimi Antonelli in 13th, appeared to have some work to do.Antonelli did not complete a qualifying simulation lap in the second session.His first had to be abandoned when Franco Colapinto crashed his Alpine at the last corner, and his second came to grief when he made an error going into the chicane.Antonelli was complaining all session about rear brake locking, but he was on a par with Norris' time in the first sector on both laps before they were curtailed.Behind Russell, Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was sixth fastest, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and McLaren's Oscar Piastri.Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.A mixed day for Aston MartinImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lance Stroll climbs out of his Aston Martin after it spun off during first practice. The Canadian did not take part in second practiceBetween the sessions, Newey said about the new Aston Martin: "Provisional results are promising. It's only part of the package, so we'll have some more steps in Zandvoort and then further in Monza and Baku."It's the first part of our planned upgrade. We're very short on parts, so we're being careful with it and trying to learn all about it."Engine partner Honda is introducing a new engine at the Dutch Grand Prix after the summer break.The day was not all positive for Aston Martin, however. Alonso's team-mate Lance Stroll spun out of the first session with what initially appeared to be a rear suspension failure.He was then unable to take part in the second because there was not enough time to repair the car.Team representative Pedro de la Rosa said: "It is a suspension failure. We were confident it would not happen in Fernando's car. That's why we sent him out. Because of the lack of spares we couldn't repair his car on time. Some parts need to be repaired and some needed to come here."Friday practice results

schema.headline: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton leads Charles Leclerc in Ferrari one-two in Friday practice

title: Heatwave anxiety can make you feel 'incredibly helpless' - here's how to manage it
description: At the peak of the June heatwave, the warmest June on record in England, all Tavia Watts could think about was how hot it was in her two- and five-yea
body: At the peak of the June heatwave, the warmest June on record in England, all Tavia Watts could think about was how hot it was in her two- and five-year-old's bedroom - above 30C in some cases."During the heatwave, I've got a high level of anxiety all the time and I'm pretty much useless," she told the BBC. "I've had to leave bedtime when my husband reads [my kids] stories to have a little cry and to calm down, because it's just too hot in their room and I'm afraid for them."Feeling "incredibly helpless", the 36-year-old posted a short reel to her hundreds of followers on Instagram, in which she voiced her inner anxieties. To her surprise, it got more than 18,000 likes and 1,700 reposts.In the video Tavia, a stay-at-home mum living in Cheltenham, says the heat "feels like the world is literally ending", she's "terrified for [her] children's lives", and that she "wants to scream at the people not taking this seriously".Watts is not alone. A 2022 study from the University of Bath estimates that about 4.6% of people in the UK have climate anxiety, which is recognised as a form of mental distress by professional bodies and the NHS. Young people and women are among the groups most at risk, according to a study published in 2025."Anticipatory anxiety", related to heatwaves in particular, has become more common, say psychologists Dr Caroline Hickman from the University of Bath and Dr Emma Lawrance from the University of Oxford."Once people have been through a traumatic event like a flood or a heatwave, they anticipate the next one," Hickman, who offers therapy to individuals experiencing climate anxiety, told the BBC.In the UK, "now we're getting the repeat, repeat, repeat [heatwaves]. It triggers that sense that 'I can't be safe in the world, and the world can't be trusted'," she added.In June's heatwave, Hickman said she "had people saying they're going to kill themselves, I've had people saying they're going to terminate pregnancies, I've had people saying that they want to sell their houses and move somewhere cooler".Watts said that her video "clearly struck a chord with people" - including therapists posting comments about coping mechanisms - and that she wanted to help others deal with climate anxiety."It can go one of two ways. You can either just fall into doomism and think, 'What is the point?'" she said."Or you can try to do something. I sign petitions during a heatwave; I organise climate community events; I run a free children's clothes swap shop. During the last heatwave, I finally became vegetarian, because then I can tell my kids at least I tried."Lawrance had some recommendations on how to cope with climate anxiety:Talk to others: There's often "a huge perception gap between how concerned people are about climate change, and how much they think other people care", said Lawrance - meaning you might wrongly assume that you're in the minority, or even that you're alone."Make space to be kind to yourself, to tend to those emotions and know that it's coming from a place of care for the world," she added.Find a community: Lawrance recommended finding a strong social network who care about the same things, and taking positive action together. Whether it's planting a garden in your school or putting solar panels on the roof of your business, action can not only help you channel your anxiety into something positive, but can help alleviate the symptoms of anxiety too.Lawrance cited the Climate Psychology Alliance in the UK for further support, as well as groups like the Resilience Project, the Climate Cares Centre, and the Climate Majority Project.Keep yourself cool: Your physical health also affects your mental health, and being hot can also make your anxiety and mood worse, Lawrance said - so she recommended making sure to keep yourself physically cool in extreme heat."Having a cool shower, putting a cold washer on your neck, making sure you're hydrated - all of those things will help physiologically as well," she said. "There's a lot we can do - we're not powerless."

schema.headline: Heatwave anxiety can make you feel 'incredibly helpless' - here's how to manage it

title: Rodri injury: Man City and Spain star to have back surgery as Enzo Maresca brushes off transfer speculation
description: World Cup winner Rodri will have surgery on a back issue on Monday, new Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has confirmed.The 30-year-old Spain captain
body: World Cup winner Rodri will have surgery on a back issue on Monday, new Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has confirmed.The 30-year-old Spain captain guided his country to World Cup glory last week and was named the Golden Ball winner as player of the tournament.But the midfielder's last two seasons at club level were heavily disrupted -  an anterior cruciate ligament injury leaving him sidelined for the majority of the 2024-25 campaign before several setbacks last season meant he was often unavailable.The Ballon d'Or winner was back to his best at the World Cup but, speaking at his first news conference since being appointed City boss, Maresca said Rodri now needs surgery followed by recuperation."Now, [he has] surgery on Monday. Then he needs a holiday, he needs to rest and recover and then he will be back with us," the Italian coach said.Maresca did not elaborate on when Rodri might return though he did dismiss speculation around the Spaniard's future at Etihad Stadium following reports in the past week linking him with a move to Real Madrid."Around big players there are always speculations so I am not worried about that," he said."I think it is normal, also because they [Spain] won the World Cup and because he is one of the best players. I think every manager wants to have Rodri because he is a top player."Of other players still to return, Maresca said he expected to have them in the squad three or four days before City face Premier League champions Arsenal in the Community Shield on Sunday, 16 August.

schema.headline: Rodri injury: Man City and Spain star to have back surgery as Enzo Maresca brushes off transfer speculation

title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says
description: A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may
body: A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may be an attempt to "manipulate the system".Rudakubana, 19, was given a life sentence for the murder of three children - Alice da Silva Aguiar, 9, Bebe King, 6, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, 7 - and attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.On Thursday, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.Prisoners who are considered to present a risk to staff, inmates or themselves because of mental disorders can be moved to hospital under the Mental Health Act.Next Wednesday marks two years since Rudakubana carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.Lawyer Chris Walker, who represents the three bereaved families, said they "don't believe the merits" of the transfer on the basis of a mental health issue and is calling for more information from ministers."In my mind this is a new event, this is something which occurred whilst he was at prison, and we at this stage don't believe the merits of it in terms of him because I've seen no evidence at all until today which suggests he has a significant mental health disorder," Walker told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.He added: "We do have an evil person but being evil does not mean that you're suffering with psychosis of some sort."We need to know is this a single event, is this a recurring event, is this him playing the system and we need those answers."The Prison Officers' Association told the BBC that Rudakubana was transferred due to a deterioration in his mental health.Walker added in a separate statement that the news would "devastate" the families at any time but "the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".He continued: "We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."A lawyer for the families of the attack's survivors said they did not want to give "notoriety" to Rudakubana and that attention should be focused on supporting the children around the anniversary.Nicola Ryan-Donnelly of Fletchers Solicitors said: "The focus of public outrage should not be on moves that this perpetrator has made, it should be examining how we are two years on from this attack and some of these girls are still not receiving the proper psychological care and support that they should be to recover from this."Prior to Rudakubana's sentencing last year, his defence lawyer told the court no psychiatric evidence could suggest a mental disorder contributed to his actions. The court also heard how Rudakubana presented as having high functioning autism and did not have any associated learning disabilities.Stan Reiz KC added that his client had appeared to have been a "normal child" until he reached 13, adding: "However, he did make a transition from a normal, well-disciplined child to someone who was capable of committing acts of such shocking and senseless violence."Rudakubana was deemed mentally fit to be detained, interviewed and stand trial. His late guilty plea meant his mental health was not discussed in detail in court during a trial.He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.Handing down the judgement, Justice Julian Goose said: "Many who have heard the evidence might describe what he did as evil, who could dispute it? On any view, it was at least the most extreme, shocking and exceptionally serious crime."He added: "I am sure that Rudakubana had a settled and determined intention to carry out these offences, and that had he been able to, he would have killed each and every child, all 26 of them, as well as any adults who got in his way."The Southport Public Inquiry has heard evidence about Rudakubana's past interactions with mental health services throughout his life. He was under the care of Alder Hey Children's NHS Foundation Trust from 2019 until he stopped engaging with its mental health service in 2023. The inquiry heard from a senior clinician that his "lack of empathy" combined with a "fascination with violence" and neurodiversity added up to a "really toxic mix".The teenager had also been referred to the government's counter-terrorism scheme Prevent three times - but there was no evidence he held a fixed ideology or motivation.Inquiry chairman Sir Adrian Fulford said there had been a "fundamental failure" by any organisation to take ownership of the risk Rudakubana posed in the years leading up to his attack.The inquiry also found there were "strong indications", though not conclusive evidence, that prior to the attack Rudakubana had researched "mental health explanations and defences that might be available to him following a criminal prosecution".Under the Mental Health Act, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.The law requires he be transferred back to prison when he no longer requires treatment in hospital. His sentence is not being converted into a "hospital order", which would mean he stayed at Broadmoor.In May 2025, Rudakubana allegedly attacked a prison officer with boiling water. An investigation is ongoing. Confirming the transfer on Thursday, the MoJ said the families of those murdered and injured would be in the country's heart forever and "our thoughts remain with them" and said it does not change Rudakubana's sentence.A statement continued: "Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act. "Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison."Additional reporting by Ella Kipling

schema.headline: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says

title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating
description: It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.
body: It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on.Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies.Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour.These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts.In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons.The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before.What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK.While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles.The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky.At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%).It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived.The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors.The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not.This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains.There should be scope for a better deal for the UK, but it raises an interesting question about whether the government will pursue an EU-style ban. This is widely seen as a backdoor way to target China, in particular for conditions in its Xinjiang province.Last October, external the government said it "remained firmly opposed to the use of state-imposed forced labour", but that it was "considering how best to reflect this position," citing "operational and legal complexities".Since then, the UK has welcomed imports of Chinese cars, and is exploring a services trade deal with the country. The relationship with China has been a balancing act for the government.This is also one of the global stories of the tariff wars. As the US repeatedly changes its rationale for tariffs, the rest of the world is focused on trading with each other. For example, Canada increased its trade with the rest of the world by more than it lost from the US.China's total dollar trade with the US is flat in the first half of this year versus last year. Across the world it is up 21%, including 14% with the EU, 11% with the UK, and 24% with Africa.There could be pressure now to legislate for a formal ban on forced labour products. Successive governments have opted for a lighter voluntary due diligence regime.Will the US force a change in the UK and elsewhere, and what might it offer in return?Or the UK may opt to keep its precarious geopolitical position by sticking to its existing deals in medicines, metals and cars.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating

title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
description: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.She told BBC Breakfast tha
body: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment."Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market."We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England. Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing"."There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents. "We need rent controls, and we need them now."Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters". "Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time. Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property. The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".Rayner was also asked about the government's target of building 1.5 million new homes by the end of the parliament in 2029.She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the target had become more challenging to meet, pointing to increased construction costs as one of the reasons for that. "1.5 million homes is a difficult target. It was when I made the target, but I'm going to keep the target, and I'm not going to be defeated," she said.The Tories say the target is a "dead letter because of her party's taxes and red tape".During Burnham's bid to replace Sir Keir Starmer as Labour leader and prime minister, he promised to deliver the biggest programme of council house building in decades. He has also long talked about implementing reforms to property taxes, including stamp duty and council tax - though he has not specified what exactly he would change while in government.Burnham has pledged to lead a "cost of living government" and has announced a series of measures in his first week in office which he said were designed to give people "breathing space". The measures include cutting VAT on household energy bills from October and restoring a £2 bus fare cap in England, except London, from January 2027.

schema.headline: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England

title: 'Explosive diarrhoea' ripples through small midwestern community
description: Many people have experienced diarrhoea.So when it hit Nick Palmiter at the beginning of July, he didn't think much of it."I'll be alright," he said to
body: Many people have experienced diarrhoea.So when it hit Nick Palmiter at the beginning of July, he didn't think much of it."I'll be alright," he said to himself.But symptoms persisted. And as days turned into weeks, the stomach cramps became unbearable."I was absolutely in pain," Palmiter said. "And it was just to the point to where I was probably using the bathroom at least 15 to 20 times a day."The 29-year-old described the sensation as a constant pressure and bubbling, "almost like you have a balloon in your stomach".At the urging of a coworker, he finally visited an urgent care facility and, upon arrival, was told that he immediately needed to go to an emergency room.It was at the hospital that Palmiter learned he had cyclosporiasis, the intestinal illness that continues to spread across the US, infecting thousands of people in 41 states - the largest recorded outbreak in US history.Michigan has seen the most cases nationwide (over 7,000). And in Monroe County, a rural patch of land on the state's eastern boundary, where Palmiter lives, documented cases are among the highest."It makes you feel absolutely sick," Palmiter said about his experience. "Like you have nothing left to give."The county has a population of roughly 154,000. According to state figures, external, 286 people there have been infected by cyclosporiasis - which comes from ingesting the cyclospora parasite, and includes symptoms like "explosive diarrhoea".The outsized impact in this small community has caused a major rippling effect."Anxiety" and "scared" were the words Palmiter used to describe the mood locally.His mother, Michelle Palmiter, said similarly."I'm seeing a lot of people that are freaking out about it," she said.That includes her niece who has cleared the entire fridge of any produce, tossing it all into the rubbish, including what Michelle saw as a perfectly good watermelon."Instead of doing a good scrub and then cutting it up, she's just throwing it out," Michelle said.Chat boards on social media for Monroe County residents show that others are going to similar lengths, reflected in comments like the one left by a mother who said she has "a whole toddler living off chicken nuggets and Goldfish [crackers] ever since this started".Michelle is still eating fruits and vegetables, but only ones she cooks. "Definitely not going out to eat at all," she said.Part of what's causing the "panic for people", she says, is how the government has fumbled its response to the outbreak."We're not trusting anything they're putting out about it."The infections were first detected on 13 May, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The number of cases has only risen since. So has the sense of mystery. Restaurants and major retailers across America – including Walmart, Jack in the Box and Taco Bell – have announced they're pulling food from shelves. "Out of an abundance of caution," has been the message. The primary target is iceberg lettuce, but, months later, the official source of cyclospora remains unknown.Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, director of the Center for Food Safety at the University of Georgia College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences, said the parasite can be "really hard to detect".Part of the difficulty has to do with gene sequencing, he explained. The other challenge is that symptoms from the parasite can take weeks to appear, making it hard for investigators to accurately trace back everything someone has eaten in order to pinpoint a common link.FDA investigations have pointed to Taylor Farms as a possible source, and the company – a major US food supplier – has voluntarily recalled all of its iceberg lettuce from central Mexico. "In an abundance of caution," they've said.The investigation appeared to reach a breakthrough on Saturday, when the FDA announced that an iceberg lettuce sample from Taylor Farms tested positive for cyclospora. But the government retracted that position less than 24-hours later, saying on Sunday that it was a false-positive."We're dealing with a pathogen that is really hard to work in the laboratory," Diez-Gonzalez said."In this case, finding a few cysts of cyclospora in a lettuce sample is literally like looking for a needle in a haystack," he continued. "It's not easy."Finding a false-positive was not unordinary, Diez-Gonzalez said. However, hearing about it was. He explained that's because test results aren't typically made public without multiple rounds of testing to corroborate findings – "to make sure that the positive is indeed a positive"."Whether they had sufficient evidence to actually go public, that's what is questionable," he said.The FDA did not return the BBC's request for comment before deadline.Extra precautions around testing are important, he continued, because inconsistencies risk "making the consumer really wary that we don't have anybody to trust".On Tuesday, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr said cyclosporiasis was "under control". That same day the Center for Disease Control and Prevention announced , externalits highest tally of cyclosporiasis yet, citing 4,173 confirmed cases and 7,400 more under investigation."Many of the additional cases" were reported in Ohio and Michigan, the CDC said.In Monroe County, Brian Clare counts himself among those infected. Though he's never been officially diagnosed, he has eaten raspberries – on the list of foods to watch – the only produce he's had in months. He said he also knows at least five other people locally with cyclosporiasis.Clare has been dealing with symptoms for over three weeks. These include repeatedly waking up throughout the night to relieve himself and "stomach aches real bad"."This is the most painful thing I've ever been through in my life," the 52-year-old said.For Clare, a grain and beef farmer, coping with the illness has required bringing rolls of toilet paper with him atop his tractor. And if the moment calls, "pop a squat in the middle of the field"."When you think you gotta go, you got less than two minutes," he said. "It's going no matter what."There is an antibiotic available that is known to curb symptoms, which Clare heard has helped a friend. But he hasn't sought medical attention himself yet."I've not got time to go to no freaking doctor," he said. "Most farmers try to self-medicate anyway. We don't have the best insurance in the world."Cyclosporiasis has taught Clare some hard lessons, like the importance of cleaning fruit and vegetables before consumption, which he "never" used to do. And, also, paying close attention to where he gets them from."I'm never buying raspberries in the store for the rest of my life, ever," Clare said. "It's been that miserable."

schema.headline: 'Explosive diarrhoea' ripples through small midwestern community

title: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
description: "We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing s
body: "We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.On Thursday, it was business rates in England; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills.Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No10 North in Manchester.Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of "the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen, external" and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that – he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead – both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him. He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.She teased the new prime minister over his informal style – he "seems like a nice guy…I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin."Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.Firstly, on the domestic front – his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options – which criminals to free first.Secondly, on the international front – after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again.Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe. Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister? Given the intended long term home of No10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032, this is a live question.And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all – that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model". It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one – where is your mandate for doing this?The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction. It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.In other words, whether he is popular enough.Let's see.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
